How forged railroad rail spikes are made

In the DoItYourself (DIY) https://voat.co/v/DIY/ https://voat.co/v/DIY/comments/1258156 was someone showcasing their skill at making knives from rail spikes. I have seen other posts here and on reddit about knife and tool making from rail spikes. I decided to expand on the making of the rail spike itself to show why these are excellent raw material for the do it yourself person.

In 1973 I worked as a Motor Inspector (Industrial Maintenance Electrician) for Colorado Fuel & Iron Corp. in Pueblo, Colorado. I 'floated' from mill to mill for troubleshooting and repair of electrical equipment and worked on some very old steel-making equipment. One of the mills I worked in forged various products, among them rail spikes. Rail spikes then (and likely still) are forged steel. They are very tough steel. I took the time to watch the craftsmen work and to talk to them. It was fascinating to do this. This experience enables me to know what to search for.

With nothing better to do tonight I found some videos on the process of forging rail spikes. I had a lot of interesting experiences working there. The oldest electric motor that I worked on had a casting date of 1878. The steam engine used to roll rail was 22,500 horsepower and it was the largest west of the Mississippi River. There is no flywheel on a steam engine--just pure torque in both directions. It can stop on a dime and reverse direction almost instantly. I digress. I prefer to see the direct links so here you are:

https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=how+things+are+made+rail+spikes

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZN8B0xzdEp4

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jYAGKyYBMEg This is as close to what I remember. Funny that I can remember what I worked on 40 years ago and have trouble remembering yesterday.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wEmpWX02dv8 Slow motion

BTW, the best rail steel is the <40' pieces used in the rail switches between two sets of tracks. That has to be quality steel because it has to take the stress and wear of the train changing direction. Some of the pieces were about 20' long.

https://youtu.be/m5gbr5DHHnY?t=36 How rail is made

The equipment originally ran from steam engines with a jack shaft along one wall of the building and belts down to the machine. An operator controlled a cog arrangement to start and stop the machine. Some of the machinery was upwards of 100 years old and had been converted to electric motors at some point. Bearings were poured babbit hand-fitted by the millwrights.
